blocks.text: A 70-year-old who falls and breaks a wrist will heal in weeks because bone is vascular and constantly remodelled, yet the same person's worn knee cartilage will not repair itself because cartilage has no blood supply. Matrix and blood supply explain both outcomes.

blocks.markdown: Histology is easiest to remember when the **extracellular matrix** is tied to function. Cartilage has **chondrocytes** in lacunae within a hydrated matrix of proteoglycans and collagen; it is **avascular**, so nutrients diffuse through the matrix, usually from the surrounding perichondrium. Bone is mineralised connective tissue with a rich blood supply. In both, the cells make and maintain the matrix and the matrix determines the mechanical behaviour.

blocks.title: Core definitions
blocks.text: Cartilage is a connective tissue with chondrocytes in lacunae in a firm, hydrated matrix. Bone is a mineralised connective tissue whose matrix is type I collagen plus hydroxyapatite (calcium phosphate crystal). An osteon (Haversian system) is the cylindrical structural unit of compact bone: concentric lamellae around a central Haversian canal.

rows: Type II; fibres not obvious on routine stains
Glassy, homogeneous matrix; chondrocytes in lacunae, often in isogenous groups
Articular surfaces (no perichondrium there), costal cartilage, nasal septum, trachea, larynx, fetal skeleton
Type II plus dense elastic fibre network
Like hyaline but elastic fibres seen with elastic stains
Thick collagen bundles, chondrocytes in rows, no distinct perichondrium
Intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis, menisci, tendon-bone junctions
blocks.caption: The three cartilage types

blocks.title: Naming a cartilage slide
blocks.prompt: A section shows rounded chondrocytes in lacunae within a smooth, glassy matrix, no obvious fibres, taken from a tracheal ring. What cartilage is this and why?

steps.text: Chondrocytes in lacunae establish that the tissue is cartilage.
A glassy matrix without visible fibres or thick collagen bundles points to hyaline cartilage, and tracheal rings are a standard hyaline site.
Elastic cartilage would show an elastic fibre network on a special stain, and fibrocartilage would show coarse type I collagen bundles with rows of cells; neither is present.

blocks.markdown: Compact bone is built of **osteons**, each roughly 200-300 micrometres in diameter, aligned along the long axis of the bone. A typical osteon has about 4-20 **concentric lamellae**, each 3-7 micrometres thick, so the wall is about 60-100 micrometres thick. The central **Haversian canal** (about 40-60 micrometres across) carries a capillary and nerve fibres. **Volkmann canals** run obliquely and link Haversian canals. Between osteons lie angular **interstitial lamellae**, remnants of older osteons. **Osteocytes** sit in **lacunae** between lamellae and contact one another through **canaliculi**.

**Scale bars.** A micrograph usually carries a scale bar of known length. True size = (measured length of object / measured length of scale bar) x (stated length of scale bar). For example, a 50 micrometre bar drawn 25 mm long and a cell measuring 10 mm gives $10/25 \times 50 = 20$ micrometres.

blocks.title: Identifying bone structures
blocks.prompt: A transverse section of compact bone shows circular units of rings, each with a small central canal. Between the rings are small dark spaces with fine radiating lines. Name the structures.

steps.text: Each ring-and-canal unit is an osteon.
The rings are concentric lamellae, layers of mineralised matrix whose collagen orientation alternates between neighbouring layers.
The central canal is the Haversian canal; the small dark spaces are lacunae holding osteocytes and the fine lines are canaliculi.

blocks.answer: Osteon, concentric lamellae, Haversian canal, lacunae and canaliculi.

blocks.markdown: **Bone remodelling.** Three cell types cooperate. **Osteoclasts** are large multinucleated cells derived from the monocyte-macrophage lineage; sitting in a resorption pit (Howship lacuna), they use a ruffled border to secrete acid that dissolves hydroxyapatite and enzymes that digest the collagen. **Osteoblasts**, derived from mesenchymal stem cells, then lay down **osteoid**, the unmineralised type I collagen matrix, and promote its mineralisation. Osteoblasts that become buried in matrix differentiate into **osteocytes**, which sense mechanical strain through their canalicular network and signal to osteoblasts and osteoclasts to direct where remodelling occurs.

items: Resorption: osteoclasts remove old or microdamaged matrix.
Formation: osteoblasts deposit osteoid, which then mineralises.
Sensing: osteocytes detect load and microdamage and coordinate the process.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A Haversian canal is the central vascular channel of an osteon, whereas a lacuna is a small cavity housing one osteocyte. Fibrocartilage is not a stronger hyaline cartilage: it is a separate tissue dominated by type I collagen.

points: Hyaline cartilage (type II, glassy) lines joints and forms trachea and costal cartilage; elastic cartilage has elastic fibres (auricle, epiglottis); fibrocartilage has type I bundles (discs, menisci).
An osteon has about 4-20 lamellae around a Haversian canal, wall about 60-100 micrometres, with osteocytes in lacunae joined by canaliculi.
Remodelling couples osteoclast resorption, osteoblast osteoid deposition and osteocyte mechanosensing; true sizes on images come from the scale bar.

questions.stem: A section from the epiglottis stains with an elastic stain and shows chondrocytes in lacunae within a dense network of branching fibres. Which tissue is this?

distractorRationale.b: Hyaline lacks a visible elastic network.
distractorRationale.c: Fibrocartilage has thick type I collagen bundles instead.
distractorRationale.d: Chondrocytes in lacunae show this is cartilage.

questions.explanation: The epiglottis is a standard site of elastic cartilage, whose elastic fibre network lets it bend and spring back. Chondrocytes in lacunae confirm cartilage rather than dense connective tissue.

questions.stem: On a transverse section of long-bone shaft, which feature is most characteristic of compact bone?

options.text: Concentric lamellae around a central Haversian canal
Rows of chondrocytes between thick collagen bundles
Adipocytes within a reticular fibre meshwork
A smooth glassy matrix with isogenous groups of cells

questions.correctOptionText: Concentric lamellae around a central Haversian canal

distractorRationale.c: This describes marrow or reticular tissue.

questions.explanation: Compact bone is organised into osteons, each with concentric lamellae around a Haversian canal. The other options describe cartilage and marrow tissues.

questions.stem: A micrograph of articular cartilage has a scale bar labelled 100 micrometres that measures 40 mm on the printed image. A chondrocyte lacuna measures 9 mm across. Calculate its true diameter in micrometres.
questions.explanation: True size = (9 / 40) x 100 = 22.5 micrometres, within the usual 10-30 micrometre range for chondrocytes. The scale bar supplies the conversion so no magnification needs to be guessed.

questions.stem: Compare hyaline cartilage and fibrocartilage in terms of collagen, microscopic appearance, one location each and mechanical role.
markingGuide: Hyaline: type II collagen, glassy homogeneous matrix.
Fibrocartilage: type I collagen, thick bundles with rows of chondrocytes.
Hyaline location, e.g. articular surface, trachea, costal cartilage.
Fibrocartilage location, e.g. intervertebral disc, meniscus, pubic symphysis.
Hyaline gives smooth compression-resistant support; fibrocartilage resists tension and absorbs shock.
questions.explanation: A strong answer links the collagen type to the appearance and the function. Listing sites alone does not demonstrate the structure-function relationship.

questions.stem: A patient with a lytic bone disease has excessive activity of the cell that dissolves hydroxyapatite using acid secreted across a ruffled border. Which cell is this?
questions.explanation: Osteoclasts are multinucleated cells with a ruffled border that acidify the resorption pit to dissolve mineral and digest collagen. Osteoblasts do the opposite job of forming new matrix.

questions.stem: In a transverse section of compact bone, a Haversian canal is 40 micrometres across and the whole osteon is 220 micrometres across. Assuming the canal is central, calculate the thickness of the lamellar wall on one side in micrometres.
questions.explanation: Lamellae surround the canal on both sides, so the wall is (220 - 40) / 2 = 90 micrometres. This lies within the expected 60-100 micrometre range for an osteon wall.

questions.stem: Which statement about bone remodelling is correct?

options.text: Osteoclasts derive from the monocyte-macrophage lineage, whereas osteoblasts derive from mesenchymal stem cells
Osteoclasts derive from osteoblasts that become buried in matrix
Osteocytes derive from osteoclasts that stop resorbing
Osteoblasts derive from the myeloid lineage and are multinucleated

questions.correctOptionText: Osteoclasts derive from the monocyte-macrophage lineage, whereas osteoblasts derive from mesenchymal stem cells

distractorRationale.b: Buried osteoblasts become osteocytes, not osteoclasts.

questions.explanation: Resorbing and forming cells have different origins: osteoclasts are haemopoietic (monocyte-macrophage lineage) and multinucleated, osteoblasts are mesenchymal. Osteocytes are osteoblasts that became embedded in matrix.

questions.stem: Explain how osteoblasts, osteocytes and osteoclasts cooperate in remodelling of compact bone.
markingGuide: Osteoclasts resorb old or damaged matrix by acid and enzymes.
Osteoblasts deposit osteoid (type I collagen) and promote its mineralisation.
Some osteoblasts become trapped and differentiate into osteocytes.
Osteocytes sense strain or microdamage via canaliculi and signal to direct remodelling.
Resorption is coupled to formation in sequence.
questions.explanation: Bone is continually broken down and rebuilt. Full marks need the role of each cell and the coupling between them.

questions.stem: In a section of long bone, a small cavity containing a cell lies between two lamellae, and a thin channel runs from it toward the central vessel. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: Cavity = Haversian canal; thin channel = lacuna

distractorRationale.b: The Haversian canal is the large central vascular channel.
distractorRationale.d: An osteon is a whole unit and a lamella a matrix layer.

questions.explanation: A lacuna holds one osteocyte, and canaliculi are the fine channels carrying its processes to neighbouring cells and the Haversian canal. These must not be confused with the much larger Haversian canal.

questions.stem: Explain why a torn knee meniscus and a fractured tibia differ in their capacity to heal, using the tissue structure of each.
markingGuide: Meniscus is fibrocartilage, largely avascular, with nutrients by diffusion and little repair capacity.
Bone is vascular, with Haversian and Volkmann canals supplying cells.
Bone has osteoclasts, osteoblasts and osteocytes enabling continuous remodelling and repair.
Links matrix and blood supply to repair ability.
questions.explanation: Avascular cartilage depends on diffusion and has few cells to mount repair, while vascular bone has a coupled remodelling system. Answers must connect structure to repair.
